questions.q: A solenoid of 1000 turns is wound uniformly on a glass tube 4 m long and $0.3$ m in diameter. The magnetic intensity at the centre of the solenoid when a current of 4 A flows through it is
questions.solution:
Given $N = 1000$, $L = 4\ \text{m}$, $I = 4\ \text{A}$.

The number of turns per unit length is $n = \dfrac{N}{L} = \dfrac{1000}{4} = 250\ \textm^{-1}$.

The magnetic intensity $H$ at the centre of a long solenoid is given by $H = nI$.

Substituting the given values:

$H = 250 \times 4 = 1000\ \text{A/m} = 10^{3}\ \text{A/m}$.

Answer: $10^{+3}\ \text{A/m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A circular arc of wire of radius of curvature $r$ subtends an angle of $\dfrac{\pi}{5}$ radian at its centre. If current $i$ is flowing in it then the magnetic induction at its centre is ($\mu_0$ = permeability of free space)
questions.solution:
The magnetic field at the centre of a circular arc subtending an angle $\theta$ at the centre is given by

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 i}{4 \pi r} \theta$

Given that the angle subtended by the arc is $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{5}$ radian.

Substituting the value of $\theta$ in the formula, we get

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 i}{4 \pi r} \times \dfrac{\pi}{5}$

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 i}{20 r}$

Answer: $\dfrac{\mu_0 i}{20r}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A thin circular wire carrying current $I$ has magnetic moment $M$. The shape of the wire is changed to a square and it carries the same current. It will have magnetic moment $M_1$. The ratio $M$ to $M_1$ is
questions.solution:
Let the length of the wire be $L$.

For the circular wire of radius $r$, the circumference is $L = 2\pi r \Rightarrow r = \dfrac{L}{2\pi}$.

The magnetic moment of the circular loop is $M = I A_c = I (\pi r^2) = I \pi \left(\dfrac{L}{2\pi}\right)^2 = \dfrac{I L^2}{4\pi}$.

For the square wire of side $a$, the perimeter is $L = 4a \Rightarrow a = \dfrac{L}{4}$.

The magnetic moment of the square loop is $M_1 = I A_s = I (a^2) = I \left(\dfrac{L}{4}\right)^2 = \dfrac{I L^2}{16}$.

The ratio of the magnetic moments is $\dfrac{M}{M_1} = \dfrac{\dfrac{I L^2}{4\pi}}{\dfrac{I L^2}{16}} = \dfrac{16}{4\pi} = \dfrac{4}{\pi}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{4}{\pi}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An electron is moving with initial velocity $\vec{v} = V_0\hat{j}$ in a magnetic field $\vec{B} = B_0\hat{i}$. Its de-Broglie wavelength will
questions.solution:
The magnetic force acting on a moving charge is given by $\vec{F} = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$.

Since the magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity vector, the work done by the magnetic field on the electron is zero.

According to the work-energy theorem, the kinetic energy of the electron remains constant, which implies its speed $v$ remains constant.

The de-Broglie wavelength is given by $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{mv}$.

Since the speed $v$ is constant, the de-Broglie wavelength of the electron remains constant.

Answer: remains constant.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A long solenoid carrying a current produces a magnetic field '$B$' along its axis. If the currunt is tripled and the number of turns per cm is halved then new value of magnetic field will be
questions.solution:
The magnetic field produced by a long solenoid along its axis is given by $B = \mu_0 n I$, where $n$ is the number of turns per unit length and $I$ is the current.

Given that the new current is $I' = 3I$ and the new number of turns per unit length is $n' = \dfrac{n}{2}$.

The new magnetic field $B'$ is:

$B' = \mu_0 n' I'$

$B' = \mu_0 \left(\dfrac{n}{2}\right) (3I)$

$B' = \dfrac{3}{2} \mu_0 n I$

$B' = \dfrac{3}{2} B$

Answer: $\dfrac{3}{2}B$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A square loop ABCD of side L carrying a current $I_1$ is placed at a distance $(L/3)$ from a conductor coplaner with a straight conductor XY carrying current $I_2$ as shown in figure. The net force on the loop will be ($\mu_0$ = magnetic permeability)
questions.solution:
The magnetic field produced by the straight wire XY at a distance $r$ is given by $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_2}{2\pi r}$, directed into the plane of the paper.

The force on the side AB of the square loop, which is at a distance $r = \dfrac{L}{3}$ and carries current $I_1$ in the same direction as $I_2$, is attractive:

$F_{AB} = I_1 L B_{AB} = I_1 L \left( \dfrac{\mu_0 I_2}{2\pi (L/3)} \right) = \dfrac{3\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi}$

The force on the side CD, which is at a distance $r = \dfrac{L}{3} + L = \dfrac{4L}{3}$ and carries current $I_1$ in the opposite direction to $I_2$, is repulsive:

$F_{CD} = I_1 L B_{CD} = I_1 L \left( \dfrac{\mu_0 I_2}{2\pi (4L/3)} \right) = \dfrac{3\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{8\pi}$

The forces on the sides BC and DA are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, so they cancel each other out.

The net force on the square loop is the difference between $F_{AB}$ and $F_{CD}$ (directed towards the straight wire):

$F_{net} = F_{AB} - F_{CD} = \dfrac{3\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi} - \dfrac{3\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{8\pi}$

$F_{net} = \dfrac{12\mu_0 I_1 I_2 - 3\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{8\pi} = \dfrac{9\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{8\pi}$

Answer: $\dfrac{9\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{8\pi}$

questions.q:
The magnetic induction produced inside an ideal solenoid, depends on which of the following quantities ?
(a) number of turns per unit length.
(b) radius of the wire.
(c) current flowing throught it.
(d) permeability of the medium.
questions.solution:
The magnetic induction inside an ideal solenoid is given by the formula $B = \mu n I$.

Here, $\mu$ is the permeability of the medium inside the solenoid, $n$ is the number of turns per unit length, and $I$ is the current flowing through the solenoid.

The magnetic induction does not depend on the radius of the wire or the radius of the solenoid.

Thus, it depends on the number of turns per unit length, the current flowing through it, and the permeability of the medium.

Answer: (a), (c) and (d)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A current carrying circular coil of radius 'R' produces magnetic field $B_1$ at an axial point P at a distance 'x' from its centre and $B_2$ at point Q placed at its centre respectively. If $B_2 = 8B_1$, the value of x is
questions.solution:
Magnetic field at an axial point P at a distance $x$ from the centre of a circular coil of radius $R$ is given by:

$B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}}$

Magnetic field at the centre Q of the coil is given by:

$B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$

Given that $B_2 = 8B_1$, substituting the expressions for $B_1$ and $B_2$:

$\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R} = 8 \left( \dfrac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}} \right)

\dfrac{1}{R} = \dfrac{8R^2}{(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}}

$(R² + x²)^{3/2} = 8R^3$

Taking the cube root on both sides:

$(R² + x²)^{1/2} = 2R$

Squaring both sides:

$R^2 + x² = 4R^2$

$x^2 = 3R^2$

$x = $\sqrt{3}$ R$

Answer: \sqrt{3}$\,R

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two thin long parallel wires, $W_1$ and $W_2$ separated by distance '$a$', carry currents $i$ and $3i$ respectively in the same direction. The magnitude of the force per unit length exerted by wire $W_1$ on wire $W_2$ is
questions.solution:
The magnetic field produced by wire $W_1$ at the position of wire $W_2$ is

$B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 i}{2\pi a}$

The magnetic force experienced by wire $W_2$ per unit length is

$\dfrac{F}{L} = B_1 I_2$

Substituting $I_2 = 3i$, we get

$\dfrac{F}{L} = \left(\dfrac{\mu_0 i}{2\pi a}\right) (3i) = \dfrac{3\mu_0 i^2}{2\pi a}$

Answer: $\dfrac{3\mu_0\, i^2}{2\pi\, a}$

questions.q: Two circular coils X (smaller) and Y (bigger), each having a single turn, carry equal currents in the same direction and subtend the same angle at point 'O' along the axis of the coil. The distances of the centers of coil to point 'O' are d and $\left(\dfrac{d}{2}\right)$ for coil Y and X respectively. The radii of coils Y and X are $(2r) and (r)$ respectively. The magnetic induction due to the bigger coil at point 'O' is $B_y$ and that due to smaller coil X at point 'O' is $B_x$. ($d \gg r$) The relation between $B_x and B_y$ is
questions.solution:
The magnetic field on the axis of a circular coil of radius $R$ at a distance $x$ from its center is given by:

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}}$

For coil Y (bigger coil):
Radius $R_y = 2r$, distance $x_y = d$.

$B_y = \dfrac{\mu_0 I (2r)^2}{2((2r)^2 + d^2)^{3/2}} = \dfrac{4\mu_0 I r^2}{2(4r^2 + d^2)^{3/2}} = \dfrac{2\mu_0 I r^2}{(4r^2 + d^2)^{3/2}}$

For coil X (smaller coil):
Radius $R_x = r$, distance $x_x = \dfrac{d}{2}$.

$B_x = \dfrac{\mu_0 I r^2}{2\left(r^2 + \left(\dfrac{d}{2}\right)^2\right)^{3/2}} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I r^2}{2\left(\dfrac{4r^2 + d^2}{4}\right)^{3/2}} = \dfrac{8\mu_0 I r^2}{2(4r^2 + d^2)^{3/2}} = \dfrac{4\mu_0 I r^2}{(4r^2 + d^2)^{3/2}}$

Comparing the expressions for $B_x$ and $B_y$, we get:

$B_x = 2B_y$

Answer: $B_x = 2B_y$

questions.q: Two wires with current 3A and 1.5A are enclosed in a circular loop P. Third parallel wire with current 1A is situated outside the loop as shown. All the wires are perpendicular to the plane of the circular loop. The value of $\oint \vec{B} \cdot \vec{dl}$ around the loop is ($\mu_0 = $ permeability of free space)
questions.solution:
According to Ampere's circuital law, the line integral of the magnetic field $\vec{B}$ around any closed loop is equal to $\mu_0$ times the net current enclosed by the loop:

$\oint \vec{B} \cdot d\vec{l} = \mu_0 I_{\text{enclosed}}$

From the given figure, the loop P encloses two wires carrying currents $3\text{ A}$ (upwards) and $1.5\text{ A}$ (downwards). The third wire carrying $1\text{ A}$ is outside the loop and does not contribute to the enclosed current.

Taking the upward direction as positive, the net enclosed current is:

$I_{\text{enclosed}} = 3 - 1.5 = 1.5\text{ A}$

Therefore, the value of the integral is:

$\oint \vec{B} \cdot d\vec{l} = \mu_0 (1.5) = 1.5\mu_0$

Answer: $1.5\,\mu_0$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A straight long wire is carrying current I. The ratio of magnetic field due to this wire at perpendicular distance 2 cm and 5 cm respectively from the wire is
questions.solution:
The magnetic field due to a long straight wire carrying current $I$ at a perpendicular distance $r$ is given by $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2 \pi r}$.

This implies that $B \propto \dfrac{1}{r}$.

Given $r_1 = 2\text{ cm}$ and $r_2 = 5\text{ cm}$.

The ratio of the magnetic fields is $\dfrac{B_1}{B_2} = \dfrac{r_2}{r_1} = \dfrac{5}{2}$.

Thus, the required ratio is $5:2$.

Answer: $5:2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle of charge '$q$' and mass '$m$' moves in a circular orbit of radius '$r$' with angular speed '$\omega$'. The ratio of the magnitude of its magnetic moment to that of its angular momentum depends upon
questions.solution:
Magnetic moment of the revolving charge is given by $M = IA$

Current $I = \dfrac{q}{T} = \dfrac{q\omega}{2\pi}$

Area $A = \pi r^2$

$M = \left(\dfrac{q\omega}{2\pi}\right)(\pi r^2) = \dfrac{1}{2}q\omega r^2$

Angular momentum of the particle is $L = mvr = m(\omega r)r = m\omega r^2$

The ratio of the magnitude of magnetic moment to that of angular momentum is $\dfrac{M}{L} = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2}q\omega r^2}{m\omega r^2} = \dfrac{q}{2m}$

This ratio depends only on $q$ and $m$.

Answer: q and m

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The ratio of magnetic field at the centre of the current carrying circular loop and its magnetic moment is '$x$'. When both the current and radius are tripled, then the ratio will be
questions.solution:
Magnetic field at the centre of a circular loop is $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$

Magnetic moment of the loop is $M = I \pi R^2$

The ratio is $x = \dfrac{B}{M} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R \cdot I \pi R^2} = \dfrac{\mu_0}{2 \pi R^3}$

When current and radius are tripled, $I' = 3I$ and $R' = 3R$

New magnetic field $B' = \dfrac{\mu_0 (3I)}{2(3R)} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R} = B$

New magnetic moment $M' = (3I) \pi (3R)^2 = 27 I \pi R^2 = 27 M$

New ratio $x' = \dfrac{B'}{M'} = \dfrac{B}{27M} = \dfrac{x}{27}$

Answer: $\dfrac{x}{27}$

questions.solution:
The magnetic field at point $O$ is the vector sum of the magnetic fields produced by the three segments of the current-carrying wire: the semi-infinite straight wire $AB$, the quarter-circular arc $BC$, and the semi-infinite straight wire $CD$.

For the semi-infinite straight wire $AB$, the perpendicular distance from $O$ is $r$. One end of the wire is at $B$ (subtending angle $0^\circ$) and the other extends to infinity (subtending angle $90^\circ$). The magnitude of the magnetic field at $O$ is:
$B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r} (\sin 90^\circ + \sin 0^\circ) = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r}$
By the right-hand rule, the direction of this field is out of the plane of the paper.

For the quarter-circular arc $BC$ of radius $r$, the angle subtended at the center $O$ is $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$. The magnitude of the magnetic field at $O$ is:
$B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi} \dfrac{(\pi/2)}{r} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r} \left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$
The current flows from $B$ to $C$ in a counter-clockwise sense relative to $O$. By the right-hand rule, the direction of this field is also out of the plane of the paper.

For the semi-infinite straight wire $CD$, the perpendicular distance from $O$ is $r$. One end is at $C$ (subtending angle $0^\circ$) and the other extends to infinity (subtending angle $90^\circ$). The magnitude of the magnetic field at $O$ is:
$B_3 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r} (\sin 90^\circ + \sin 0^\circ) = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r}$
By the right-hand rule, the direction of this field is out of the plane of the paper.

Since all three magnetic field components are in the same direction, the net magnetic field at $O$ is their sum:
$B_{net} = B_1 + B_2 + B_3$
$B_{net} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r} + \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r} \left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) + \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r}$
$B_{net} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r} \left(1 + \dfrac{\pi}{2} + 1\right) = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r} \left(2 + \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$

Answer: $\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{I}{r}\left(2+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$

questions.q: In the cyclotron, as radius of the circular path of the charged particle increases, (\omega$ = angular velocity, V = linear velocity)$
questions.solution:
The centripetal force required for circular motion is provided by the magnetic force.

$\dfrac{m V^2}{r} = q V B$

$V = \dfrac{q B r}{m}$

Since $q$, $B$, and $m$ are constant, $V \propto r$. Thus, as the radius $r$ increases, the linear velocity $V$ increases.

The angular velocity $\omega$ is given by:

$\omega = \dfrac{V}{r} = \dfrac{q B}{m}$

Since $q$, $B$, and $m$ are constant, $\omega$ remains constant.

Answer: V increases , $\omega$ remains constant.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The magnetic field at a distance 'r' from a long straight wire carrying current I is 0.4 tesla. The magnetic field at a distance 2r will be
questions.solution:
The magnetic field due to a long straight wire carrying current $I$ at a distance $r$ is given by $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2 \pi r}$.

This implies that $B \propto \dfrac{1}{r}$.

Let the magnetic field at distance $r$ be $B_1 = 0.4$ T.

At distance $2r$, the magnetic field $B_2$ will be:

$\dfrac{B_2}{B_1} = \dfrac{r}{2r} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

$B_2 = \dfrac{B_1}{2} = \dfrac{0.4}{2} = 0.2$ T.

Answer: $0 \cdot 2$ tesla

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two wires of same length are bent to form the circular loop with two turns and a square loop of one turn. Both of them carry same current. The ratio of magnetic moment of circular loop of two turns to that of square loop is
questions.solution:
Let the length of the wire be $L$ and the current be $I$.

For the circular loop with two turns, the total length is $2 \times 2\pi r = L$, which gives $r = \dfrac{L}{4\pi}$.

The magnetic moment of the circular loop is $M_1 = N_1 I A_1 = 2 I (\pi r^2) = 2 I \pi \left(\dfrac{L}{4\pi}\right)^2 = \dfrac{I L^2}{8\pi}$.

For the square loop with one turn, the perimeter is $4a = L$, which gives $a = \dfrac{L}{4}$.

The magnetic moment of the square loop is $M_2 = N_2 I A_2 = 1 I a^2 = I \left(\dfrac{L}{4}\right)^2 = \dfrac{I L^2}{16}$.

The ratio of their magnetic moments is $\dfrac{M_1}{M_2} = \dfrac{\dfrac{I L^2}{8\pi}}{\dfrac{I L^2}{16}} = \dfrac{16}{8\pi} = \dfrac{2}{\pi}$.

Answer: $2 : \pi$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The magnetic field at perpendicular distance '$r$' from a long wire carrying current '$I$' is '$B$'. The magnetic field at perpendicular distance '$2r$' from the same wire is
questions.solution:
The magnetic field produced by a long straight wire carrying current $I$ at a perpendicular distance $r$ is given by:

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$

This relation shows that the magnetic field is inversely proportional to the perpendicular distance from the wire:

$B \propto \dfrac{1}{r}$

Let the magnetic field at distance $r_1 = r$ be $B_1 = B$.

Let the magnetic field at distance $r_2 = 2r$ be $B_2$.

Taking the ratio of the magnetic fields:

$\dfrac{B_2}{B_1} = \dfrac{r_1}{r_2}$

$\dfrac{B_2}{B} = \dfrac{r}{2r}$

$\dfrac{B_2}{B} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

$B_2 = \dfrac{B}{2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The magnetic field at the center of circular coil carrying current '$I$' for a single turn of a given length of wire is '$B$'. The same wire is bent in a circular coil having two turns. When the same current passes through it, the value of magnetic field becomes
questions.solution:
Let the length of the wire be $L$.

For a single turn coil, the radius $R_1$ is given by $2\pi R_1 = L \Rightarrow R_1 = \dfrac{L}{2\pi}$.

The magnetic field at the center of the single turn coil is $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2 R_1}$.

When the same wire is bent into a coil of $N=2$ turns, the new radius $R_2$ is given by $2 \times 2\pi R_2 = L \Rightarrow R_2 = \dfrac{L}{4\pi} = \dfrac{R_1}{2}$.

The magnetic field at the center of the two-turn coil is $B' = \dfrac{\mu_0 N I}{2 R_2}$.

Substituting $N = 2$ and $R_2 = \dfrac{R_1}{2}$, we get $B' = \dfrac{\mu_0 (2) I}{2 \left(\dfrac{R_1}{2}\right)} = 4 \left(\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2 R_1}\right) = 4B$.

Answer: $4B$

questions.solution:
The magnetic field at the center of a circular loop of radius $R$ carrying current $I$ is given by:

$B_{center} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$

The magnetic field on the axis of the circular loop at a distance $x$ from the center is given by:

$B_{axis} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}}$

Substituting $x = R$, we get:

$B_{axis} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2(R^2 + R^2)^{3/2}} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2(2R^2)^{3/2}} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2(2\sqrt{2}R^3)} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\sqrt{2}R}$

The ratio of the magnetic fields is:

$\dfrac{B_{center}}{B_{axis}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R}}{\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\sqrt{2}R}} = \dfrac{4\sqrt{2}}{2} = 2\sqrt{2} = \sqrt{8}$

The required ratio is $\sqrt{8} : 1$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The magnitude of magnetic induction at mid point 'O' due to current arrangement as shown in figure will be ($\mu_0$ = permeability of free space)
questions.solution:
From the given figure, the horizontal distance between the vertical wire segment BC and the vertical wire segment ET is $a$.

Since point O is the midpoint, the perpendicular distance from O to each of these vertical segments is $a/2$.

Assuming the horizontal wire segments AB and DE are collinear and their extended axis passes through O, the magnetic field produced by them at point O is zero.

The vertical segment BC acts as a semi-infinite straight wire with its end at the level of O. The magnetic induction at O due to BC is $B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi(a/2)} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi a}$. By the right-hand thumb rule, its direction is perpendicular to the plane of the paper, pointing outwards.

The vertical segment ET also acts as a semi-infinite straight wire with its end at the level of O. The magnetic induction at O due to ET is $B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi(a/2)} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi a}$. By the right-hand thumb rule, its direction is also perpendicular to the plane of the paper, pointing outwards.

Since both magnetic fields are in the same direction, the total magnetic induction at O is the sum of their magnitudes:

$B = B_1 + B_2$

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi a} + \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi a} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{\pi a}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The magnetic field intensity (H) at the centre of a long solenoid having 'n' turns per unit length and carrying a current I, when no material is kept in it is (\mu_0$ = permeability of free space)$
questions.solution:
The magnetic field $B$ at the centre of a long solenoid is given by $B = \mu_0 n I$, where $n$ is the number of turns per unit length and $I$ is the current.

The magnetic field intensity $H$ is related to the magnetic field $B$ in free space by the relation $H = \dfrac{B}{\mu_0}$.

Substituting the value of $B$, we get $H = \dfrac{\mu_0 n I}{\mu_0} = nI$.

Answer: $nI$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Torque acting on a coil carrying current 'I' situated parallel to magnetic field of induction 'B' having of turns 'n' and area 'A' is
questions.solution:
The magnetic moment of a current-carrying coil having $n$ turns, area $\vec{A}$, and current $I$ is given by:

$\vec{M} = nI\vec{A}$

The torque $\vec{\tau}$ acting on a magnetic dipole placed in a uniform magnetic field $\vec{B}$ is given by the cross product of the magnetic moment and the magnetic field:

$\vec{\tau} = \vec{M} \times \vec{B}$

Substituting the expression for magnetic moment into the torque equation, we get:

$\vec{\tau} = nI(\vec{A} \times \vec{B})$

Answer: $\text{nI}(\vec{A} \times \vec{B})$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A charged particle is moving in a uniform magnetic field in a circular path of radius 'R'. When the energy of the particle becomes 3 times the original, the new radius will be
questions.solution:
The radius of a charged particle moving in a uniform magnetic field is given by $R = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$.

The kinetic energy of the particle is $E = \dfrac{p^2}{2m}$, which gives the momentum $p = mv = \sqrt{2mE}$.

Substituting the momentum in the radius formula, we get $R = \dfrac{\sqrt{2mE}}{qB}$.

This shows that $R \propto \sqrt{E}$.

When the energy becomes $3$ times the original, the new energy is $E' = 3E$.

The new radius $R'$ is given by $R' = \dfrac{\sqrt{2m(3E)}}{qB} = \sqrt{3} \dfrac{\sqrt{2mE}}{qB} = \sqrt{3}R$.

Answer: $\sqrt{3}$R

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A wire carrying current 'I' along x axis has length 'L' and it is kept in a magnetic field $B(\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-2\hat{k})$ T. The magnitude of magnetic force acting on the wire is
questions.solution:
The magnetic force on a current-carrying wire is given by $\vec{F} = I(\vec{L} \times \vec{B})$.

Since the wire is along the x-axis, the length vector is $\vec{L} = L\hat{i}$.

The magnetic field is given as $\vec{B} = B(\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - 2\hat{k})$.

Substituting these into the force formula:

$\vec{F} = I[L\hat{i} \times B(\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - 2\hat{k})]$

$\vec{F} = ILB[\hat{i} \times \hat{i} + 2(\hat{i} \times \hat{j}) - 2(\hat{i} \times \hat{k})]$

Using the cross product rules $\hat{i} \times \hat{i} = 0$, $\hat{i} \times \hat{j} = \hat{k}$, and $\hat{i} \times \hat{k} = -\hat{j}$:

$\vec{F} = ILB[0 + 2\hat{k} - 2(-\hat{j})] = 2ILB(\hat{j} + \hat{k})$

The magnitude of the magnetic force is:

$|\vec{F}| = \sqrt{(2ILB)^2 + (2ILB)^2} = \sqrt{8I^2L^2B^2} = \sqrt{8}ILB$

Answer: $\sqrt{8}\,\text{ILB}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The magnetic moment produced in a sample of 2 gram is $8 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{A/m}^2$. If its density is $4\ \text{g/cm}^3$ then the magnetization of the sample is
questions.solution:
Given, mass of the sample $m = 2 \text{ g}$

Density of the sample $d = 4 \text{ g/cm}^3$

Volume of the sample $V = \dfrac{m}{d} = \dfrac{2}{4} = 0.5 \text{ cm}^3 = 0.5 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^3$

Magnetic moment $M = 8 \times 10^{-7} \text{ A m}^2$

Magnetization $I = \dfrac{M}{V}$

$I = \dfrac{8 \times 10^{-7}}{0.5 \times 10^{-6}} = 1.6 \text{ A/m}$

Answer: $1.6$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A thin ring of radius 'R' metre has charge 'q' coulomb uniformly spread on it. The ring rotates about its axis with a constant frequency of 'f' revolution/s. The value of magnetic induction at the centre of the ring in $\text{Wb/m}^2$ is

(\mu_0$ = permeability of free space )$
questions.solution:
The equivalent current $I$ due to the rotating charge is given by the rate of flow of charge.

$I = \dfrac{q}{T} = qf$

The magnetic induction at the centre of a circular current-carrying loop is given by:

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$

Substituting the value of $I$, we get:

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 qf}{2R}$

Answer: $\dfrac{\mu_0 qf}{2R}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A long wire is bent into a circular coil of one turn and then into a circular coil of smaller radius having n turns. If the same current is passed in both the cases, the ratio of magnetic field produced at the centre for one turn to that of n turns is
questions.solution:
Let the length of the wire be $L$.

For a circular coil of one turn, the radius $R_1$ is given by $L = 2 \pi R_1 \Rightarrow R_1 = \dfrac{L}{2 \pi}$.

The magnetic field at the centre of the coil of one turn is $B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2 R_1}$.

For a circular coil of $n$ turns, the radius $R_n$ is given by $L = n(2 \pi R_n) \Rightarrow R_n = \dfrac{L}{2 \pi n} = \dfrac{R_1}{n}$.

The magnetic field at the centre of the coil of $n$ turns is $B_n = \dfrac{\mu_0 n I}{2 R_n}$.

Substituting $R_n = \dfrac{R_1}{n}$, we get $B_n = \dfrac{\mu_0 n I}{2 \left(\dfrac{R_1}{n}\right)} = n^2 \left(\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2 R_1}\right) = n^2 B_1$.

The ratio of the magnetic field for one turn to that of $n$ turns is $\dfrac{B_1}{B_n} = \dfrac{1}{n^2}$.

Answer: $1 : n^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A charge moves in a circular path perpendicular to a magnetic field. The time period of revolution is independent of
questions.solution:
When a charged particle moves in a circular path perpendicular to a magnetic field, the magnetic force provides the necessary centripetal force.

$qvB = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$

The radius of the circular path is given by $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$

The time period of revolution is $T = \dfrac{2\pi r}{v}$

Substituting the value of $r$, we get $T = \dfrac{2\pi m}{qB}$

The time period depends on the mass of the particle, its charge, and the magnetic field. It is independent of the velocity of the particle.

Answer: velocity of the particle

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Lorentz magnetic force is acting on a particle of charge $q$ moving with velocity $\vec{V}$ in magnetic field $\vec{B}$. The work done by this force on the charged particle is
questions.solution:
The Lorentz magnetic force on a charged particle is given by $\vec{F} = q(\vec{V} \times \vec{B})$.

The power delivered by this force is $P = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{V} = q(\vec{V} \times \vec{B}) \cdot \vec{V}$.

Since the cross product $\vec{V} \times \vec{B}$ is always perpendicular to the velocity vector $\vec{V}$, their dot product is zero.

Thus, $P = 0$.

The work done by the magnetic force is $W = \int P dt = 0$.

Therefore, the work done by the Lorentz magnetic force on the charged particle is zero.

Answer: zero

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A circular coil of 'N' turns and diameter 'd' carries current 'I'. It is unwound and rewound to make another coil of diameter '2d', current 'I' remaining the Same. The ratio of magnetic moments of the new coil to the original coil is
questions.solution:
Length of the wire remains constant.

$L = N \times \pi d = N' \times \pi (2d)$

$N' = \dfrac{N}{2}$

Magnetic moment of the original coil is $M_1 = N I A_1 = N I \left( \dfrac{\pi d^2}{4} \right)

Magnetic moment of the new coil is $ M_2 = N' I A_2 = $\left( \dfrac{N}{2} \right)$ I $\left( \dfrac{\pi (2d)^2}{4} \right) = \dfrac{N}{2}$ I ($\pi$ d^2)

Ratio of $magnetic moments is \dfrac{M_2}{M_1} = \dfrac{\dfrac{N}{2} I \pi d^2}{N I \dfrac{\pi d^2}{4}} = \dfrac{1/2}{1/4} =2$

The ratio is $2:1$.

Answer: $2:1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The magnetic moments associated with two closely wound circular coils a and b of radius $r$ and $2r$ respectively are equal if (where $N_a$, $I_a$ and $N_b$, $I_b$ are number of turns and current in A and B respectively)
questions.solution:
The magnetic moment of a circular coil is given by $M = NIA$, where $N$ is the number of turns, $I$ is the current, and $A$ is the area of the coil.

For coil A, the area is $A_a = \pi r^2$.
The magnetic moment of coil A is $M_a = N_a I_a (\pi r^2)$.

For coil B, the area is $A_b = \pi (2r)^2 = 4\pi r^2$.
The magnetic moment of coil B is $M_b = N_b I_b (4\pi r^2)$.

Given that the magnetic moments are equal, $M_a = M_b$.

$N_a I_a (\pi r^2) = N_b I_b (4\pi r^2)$

$N_a I_a = 4N_b I_b$

Answer: $N_a I_a = 4N_b I_b$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A rod with a circular cross-section area $2$ cm^2$ and length $40$ cm is wound uniformly with $400$ turns of an insulated wire. If a current $0.4$ A flows in the wire winding, the total magnetic flux produced inside the winding is $4\pi \times 10^{-6}$ Wb. The relative permeability of the rod is
(Given permeability of vacuum $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ N m A^{-2}$)
questions.solution:
The magnetic flux $\Phi$ inside the solenoid is given by $\Phi = B A$, where $B$ is the magnetic field and $A$ is the cross-sectional area.

Substituting the given values, the magnetic field is:

$B = \dfrac{\Phi}{A} = \dfrac{4\pi \times 10^{-6}}{2 \times 10^{-4}} = 2\pi \times 10^{-2} \text{ T}$

The magnetic field inside a solenoid with a core of relative permeability $\mu_r$ is also given by:

$B = \mu_0 \mu_r n I = \mu_0 \mu_r \dfrac{N}{l} I$

Substituting the known values into the equation:

$2\pi \times 10^{-2} = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times \mu_r \times \dfrac{400}{0.4} \times 0.4$

$2\pi \times 10^{-2} = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times \mu_r \times 400$

$2\pi \times 10^{-2} = 16\pi \times 10^{-5} \times \mu_r$

Solving for $\mu_r$:

$\mu_r = \dfrac{2\pi \times 10^{-2}}{16\pi \times 10^{-5}} = \dfrac{1000}{8} = 125$

Answer: $125$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Two long straight wires are arranged parallel to each other and are kept $20$ cm apart in vacuum. They carry currents of $2$ A and $4$ A respectively in the same direction. What will be the magnetic force on a length of $10$ cm of either wire?
(\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ SI units)$
questions.solution:
The magnetic force on a length $L$ of either wire is given by the formula:

$F = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2 L}{2\pi d}$

Given:
$I_1 = 2$ A
$I_2 = 4$ A
$d = 20$ cm $= 0.2$ m
$L = 10$ cm $= 0.1$ m
$\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ T m/A

Substituting the values:

$F = \dfrac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 2 \times 4 \times 0.1}{2\pi \times 0.2}$

$F = 2 \times 10^{-7} \times \dfrac{0.8}{0.2}$

$F = 8 \times 10^{-7}$ N

Answer: $8 \times 10^{-7}$ N

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A charged particle $q$ is accelerated by a potential difference of $V$ enters a region of uniform magnetic field of induction $B$ at right angles to the direction of the field. The charged particle completes semi circle of the radius $r$ inside the magnetic field. The mass of the charged particle is (all quantities are in SI units)
questions.solution:
The kinetic energy gained by the charged particle when accelerated through a potential difference $V$ is given by $K = qV$.

The momentum of the particle is $p = \sqrt{2mK} = \sqrt{2mqV}$.

When the particle enters a uniform magnetic field $B$ perpendicularly, it moves in a circular path of radius $r$ given by $r = \dfrac{p}{qB}$.

Substituting the value of $p$, we get $r = \dfrac{\sqrt{2mqV}}{qB}$.

Squaring both sides, $r^2 = \dfrac{2mqV}{q^2 B^2} = \dfrac{2mV}{qB^2}$.

Rearranging for mass $m$, we get $m = \dfrac{q r^2 B^2}{2V}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If the number of turns in the coil of a moving coil galvanometer decreases, the resistance of the galvanometer,
questions.solution:
The resistance of a coil is given by $R = \rho \dfrac{l}{A}$.

The total length of the wire in the coil is $l = N \times \text{perimeter of one turn}$, where $N$ is the number of turns.

Thus, the resistance of the galvanometer is directly proportional to the number of turns (R \propto N$).

When the number of turns in the coil decreases, the total length of the wire decreases.

Consequently, the resistance of the galvanometer decreases.

Answer: decreases$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The magnetic flux near the axis and inside the air core solenoid of length 60 cm carrying current I is $\dfrac{\pi}{2} \times 10^{-6}$ Wb. Its magnetic moment will be (cross-sectional area is very small as compared to length of solenoid, $\mu_0$ = Permeability of free space = $4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ SI unit)
questions.solution:
The magnetic field inside a long solenoid is given by $B = \mu_0 n I = \mu_0 \dfrac{N}{L} I$.

The magnetic flux through the cross-section of the solenoid is $\Phi = B A = \mu_0 \dfrac{N I A}{L}$.

The magnetic moment of the solenoid is $M = N I A$.

Substituting $M$ into the flux equation, we get $\Phi = \dfrac{\mu_0 M}{L}$.

Rearranging for $M$, we have $M = \dfrac{\Phi L}{\mu_0}$.

Given $\Phi = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \times 10^{-6} \text{ Wb}$, $L = 60 \text{ cm} = 0.6 \text{ m}$, and $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \text{ T m/A}$.

$M = \dfrac{\dfrac{\pi}{2} \times 10^{-6} \times 0.6}{4\pi \times 10^{-7}}$

$M = \dfrac{0.3\pi \times 10^{-6}}{4\pi \times 10^{-7}}$

$M = \dfrac{0.3}{4} \times 10 = \dfrac{3}{4} = 0.75 \text{ Am}^2$

Answer: $0.75 \text{ Am}^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two parallel wires of equal lengths are separated by a distance of $3$ m from each other. The currents flowing through first and second wire is $3$ A and $4.5$ A respectively in opposite directions. The resultant magnetic field at mid point of both the wires is (\mu_0$=permeability of free space)$
questions.solution:
Distance between the wires, $d = 3$ m.

Distance of the midpoint from each wire, $r = \dfrac{d}{2} = 1.5$ m.

Current in the first wire, $I_1 = 3$ A.

Current in the second wire, $I_2 = 4.5$ A.

Since the currents are flowing in opposite directions, the magnetic fields produced by both wires at the midpoint will be in the same direction.

The resultant magnetic field at the midpoint is $B = B_1 + B_2$.

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1}{2\pi r} + \dfrac{\mu_0 I_2}{2\pi r}$

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi r} (I_1 + I_2)$

Substituting the given values:

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi (1.5)} (3 + 4.5)$

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi (1.5)} (7.5)$

$B = \dfrac{5\mu_0}{2\pi}$

Answer: $\dfrac{5\mu_0}{2\pi}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A wire AB is carrying steady current $I_1$ and is kept on the table. Another wire CD carrying current $I_2$ is held directly above as shown in figure. When the wire CD is left free and it remains suspended at its position, its mass per unit length is (g=acceleration due to gravity, $\mu_0$ = permeability of free space)
questions.solution:
The magnetic force per unit length between two parallel wires carrying currents $I_1$ and $I_2$ separated by a distance $r$ is given by:

$F_m = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi r}$

Since the currents in wires AB and CD are in opposite directions, the magnetic force between them is repulsive. This upward force on wire CD balances its downward gravitational force.

Let $\lambda$ be the mass per unit length of wire CD. The weight per unit length is:

$F_g = \lambda g$

For wire CD to remain suspended in equilibrium, the magnetic force per unit length must equal the weight per unit length:

$F_m = F_g$

$\dfrac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi r} = \lambda g$

$\lambda = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi r g}$

Answer: $\dfrac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi r g}$
questions.question: A wire AB is carrying steady current $I_1$ and is kept on the table. Another wire CD carrying current $I_2$ is held directly above as shown in figure. When the wire CD is left free and it remains suspended at its position, its mass per unit length is (g=acceleration due to gravity, $\mu_0$ = permeability of free space)
questions.explanation:
The magnetic force per unit length between two parallel wires carrying currents $I_1$ and $I_2$ separated by a distance $r$ is given by:

$F_m = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi r}$

Since the currents in wires AB and CD are in opposite directions, the magnetic force between them is repulsive. This upward force on wire CD balances its downward gravitational force.

Let $\lambda$ be the mass per unit length of wire CD. The weight per unit length is:

$F_g = \lambda g$

For wire CD to remain suspended in equilibrium, the magnetic force per unit length must equal the weight per unit length:

$F_m = F_g$

$\dfrac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi r} = \lambda g$

$\lambda = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi r g}$

Answer: $\dfrac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi r g}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A circular coil of N turns and diameter D carries current I. It is unwound and rewound to make another coil of diameter 2D, current I remaining the same. The ratio of magnetic moments of the original coil to the new coil is
questions.solution:
The length of the wire remains constant when unwound and rewound.

$L = N \pi D = N' \pi (2D)$

$N' = \dfrac{N}{2}$

The magnetic moment of a circular coil is given by $M = NIA$.

For the original coil:

$M_1 = NI \left( \dfrac{\pi D^2}{4} \right)

For the new coil:

$ M_2 = N' I $\left( \dfrac{\pi (2D)^2}{4} \right) = \left( \dfrac{N}{2} \right) I (\piD^2) = 2 NI \left( \dfrac{\pi D^2}{4} \right)$

Taking the ratio of the magnetic moments:

$\dfrac{M_1}{M_2} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

Answer: $1:2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two long parallel wires carrying currents $8$A and $15$A in opposite directions are placed at a distance of $7$ cm from each other. A point P is at equidistant from both the wires such that the lines joining the point P to the wires are perpendicular to each other. The magnetic field at P is ___ $\times 10^{-6}$ T. (Given: $\sqrt{2} =$1.4$, \mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ SI unit)
questions.solution:
Let the distance of point P from each wire be $r$. Since the lines joining P to the wires are perpendicular, they form a right-angled isosceles triangle with the distance between the wires as the hypotenuse.

$r^2 + r^2 = d^2 \Rightarrow 2r^2 = (7 \times 10^{-2})^2 \Rightarrow r = \dfrac{7}{\sqrt{2}} \times 10^{-2}$ m

The magnetic fields due to the two wires at point P are:

$B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1}{2\pi r}$ and $B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_2}{2\pi r}$

Since the position vectors from the wires to point P are perpendicular to each other, the magnetic field vectors $\vec{B}_1$ and $\vec{B}_2$ are also perpendicular to each other.

The net magnetic field at P is:

$B = \sqrt{B_1^2 + B_2^2} = \dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi r} \sqrt{I_1^2 + I_2^2}$

Substituting the given values:

$B = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-7}}{\dfrac{7}{\sqrt{2}} \times 10^{-2}} \sqrt{8^2 + 15^2}$

$B = \dfrac{2 \sqrt{2} \times 10^{-5}}{7} \times 17$

$B = \dfrac{34 \times 1.4}{7} \times 10^{-5}$

$B = 34 \times 0.2 \times 10^{-5} = 6.8 \times 10^{-5} \text{ T} = 68 \times 10^{-6} \text{ T}$

Answer: $68$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A wire of length $L$ is bent in the form of a circular coil and current '$i$' is passed through it. This coil is kept in magnetic field. The torque acting on the coil will be maximum, when the number of turns is ___
questions.solution:
The torque acting on a circular coil of $N$ turns in a magnetic field is given by $\tau = N i A B \sin \theta$.

For maximum torque, $\sin \theta = 1$, giving $\tau = N i A B$.

Let $r$ be the radius of the coil. The total length of the wire is $L = N(2 \pi r)$, which gives $r = \dfrac{L}{2 \pi N}$.

The area of the coil is $A = \pi r^2 = \pi \left( \dfrac{L}{2 \pi N} \right)^2 = \dfrac{L^2}{4 \pi N^2}$.

Substituting the area into the torque expression, we get $\tau = N i \left( \dfrac{L^2}{4 \pi N^2} \right) B = \dfrac{i L^2 B}{4 \pi N}$.

For the torque to be maximum, the number of turns $N$ must be minimum.

Since $N$ is a positive integer, the minimum possible value is $N = 1$.

Answer: $1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A wire of length ' $L$ ' carries a current ' $I$ '. If the wire is turned into a square coil of single turn, the maximum magnitude of the torque in a given magnetic field ( $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}$ ) is
questions.solution:
Maximum torque on a square coil

The magnetic dipole moment determines the torque experienced by a current-carrying loop in a magnetic field.

Using a wire of length $L$, the side length of the square coil is $a = \frac{L}{4}$, giving an area $A = a^2 = \frac{L^2}{16}$.

For a single-turn coil, the magnetic dipole moment is $M = IA = \frac{IL^2}{16}$.

The torque magnitude is $\tau = MB\sin\theta$, which reaches its maximum $\tau_{\text\max} = MB$ when $\sin\theta = 1$.

Therefore, $\tau_{\text\max} = \frac{IBL^2}{16}$.

This result corresponds to option D.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A circular coil carrying current has radius ' $R$ '. The distance from the centre of the coil on the axis where the magnetic induction will be $\frac{1}{27}$ th to its value at the centre of the coil is
questions.solution:
The magnetic induction B at distance $x$ along the axis of a circular coil of radius $R$ carrying current $I$ is given by $B_x = \frac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}}$.

At the coil’s center ($x = 0$), the magnetic field simplifies to $B_c = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$.

Given $B_x = \frac{1}{27} B_c$, substitute the expressions:
$\frac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}} = \frac{1}{27} \cdot \frac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$.

Cancel the common factors $\mu_0 I / 2$ from both sides:
$\frac{R^2}{(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}} = \frac{1}{27R}$.

Cross-multiplying yields $27R^3 = (R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}$.
Raising both sides to the power $\frac{2}{3}$ gives $(27R^3)^{2/3} = (R^2 + x^2)$.

Evaluate the left-hand side:
$(3^3 R^3)^{2/3} = 3^2 R^2 = 9R^2$, so $9R^2 = R^2 + x^2$.

Solving for $x^2$: $x^2 = 8R^2$, hence $x = \sqrt{8R^2} = 2\sqrt{2} R$.

The magnetic induction is $\frac{1}{27}$ its central value at a distance $x = 2\sqrt{2} R$ along the axis.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two long straight parallel conductors carry currents ' $\mathrm{I}_1{ }^{\prime}$ and ' $\mathrm{I}_2{ }^{\prime} \left(\mathrm{I}_1 > \mathrm{I}_2\right). When direction of ' \mathrm{I}_1 ' and ' \mathrm{I}_2 ' is same, the magnetic field intensity midway between two conductors is 20 \mu \mathrm{ T}.If direction of ' \mathrm{I}_2 ' is reversed, the field intensity becomes 50 \mu \mathrm{ T}.The ratio \mathrm{I}_2$/ $\mathrm{I}_{1}$ is
questions.solution:
The magnetic field intensity at the midway point between two parallel conductors separated by distance $d$ is considered. Each field contribution follows $B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$, with $r = d/2$ at the midpoint.

For currents flowing in the same direction, the magnetic fields oppose, yielding a net field:

$B_{\text{net}} = \frac{\mu_0}{\pi d}(I_1 - I_2) = 20\,\mu\text{T}$.

Reversing $I_2$ aligns the fields, giving:

$B_{\text{net}} = \frac{\mu_0}{\pi d}(I_1 + I_2) = 50\,\mu\text{T}$.

Dividing these equations eliminates the common factor:

$\frac{I_1 - I_2}{I_1 + I_2} = \frac{2}{5}$.

Solving yields $5(I_1 - I_2) = 2(I_1 + I_2)$, which simplifies to $3I_1 = 7I_2$.

The current ratio is therefore:

$\frac{I_2}{I_1} = \frac{3}{7}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A current carrying circular coil of radius ' R ' produces magnetic fields ' $\mathrm{B}_1$ ' and ' $\mathrm{B}_2$ ' at an axial point ' P ' at a distance ' x ' from its centre and at a point ' $Q$ ' placed at its centre respectively. If $B_1=\frac{B_2}{8}$, the value of ' $x$ ' is
questions.solution:
The magnetic field at the center of a circular coil is given by $B_2 = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$, while the field at an axial point distance $x$ from the center is $B_1 = \frac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}}$.

Given $B_1 = \frac{B_2}{8}$, substitute both expressions:

$\frac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}} = \frac{1}{8} \cdot \frac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$

Canceling common factors $\frac{\mu_0 I}{2}$ from both sides yields:

$\frac{R^2}{(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}} = \frac{1}{8R}$

Cross-multiplying gives $8R^3 = (R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}$. Raising both sides to the $2/3$ power:

$(8R^3)^{2/3} = [(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}]^{2/3}$

$(2R)^2 = R^2 + x^2$

$4R^2 = R^2 + x^2$

$3R^2 = x^2$

$x = R\sqrt{3}$

The distance where the axial field equals one-eighth the center field is $R\sqrt{3}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Lorenz magnetic force is acting on a particle of charge $q$ moving with velocity $\vec{V}$ in a magnetic field $\vec{B}$. The work done by this force on the charged particle is
questions.solution:
The Lorentz magnetic force acting on a particle of charge $q$ moving with velocity $\vec{V}$ in a magnetic field $\vec{B}$ is given by $\vec{F} = q(\vec{V} \times \vec{B})$.

By definition of the cross product, the force $\vec{F}$ is perpendicular to both $\vec{V}$ and $\vec{B}$.

The work done by a force $\vec{F}$ through displacement $d\vec{r}$ is $dW = \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r}$.
Since $d\vec{r} = \vec{V} dt$, this becomes $dW = (\vec{F} \cdot \vec{V}) dt$.

As $\vec{F}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{V}$, their dot product vanishes: $\vec{F} \cdot \vec{V} = 0$.

Consequently,
$W = \int dW = \int 0 \cdot dt = 0$.

The magnetic force does no work and therefore cannot change the particle's kinetic energy;
it only alters the direction of motion.

$\boxed{\text{zero}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two wires of equal lengths are bent in the form of a square and a circular loop. They are suspended in a uniform magnetic field and same current is passed through them. Torque experienced by
options: both the loops is same but not zero.
questions.solution:
The torque on a current loop in a uniform magnetic field is given by $\tau = NIAB\sin\theta$. For identical current $I$ and magnetic field $B$, with both loops optimally oriented ($\sin\theta = 1$), the torque depends only on area $A$ since $N=1$.

Using wire length $L$, the square side is $s = L/4$ with area $A_{\text{square}} = (L/4)^2 = L^2/16$.

The circular loop has radius $r = L/(2\pi)$ and area $A_{\text{circle}} = \pi r^2 = L^2/(4\pi)$.

Comparing areas: $L^2/(4\pi) > L^2/16$ since $4\pi \approx 12.566 < 16$. Thus $\tau_{\text{circle}} > \tau_{\text{square}}$.

Final answer: $\boxed{D}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The work done in turning a magnet of magnetic moment ' M ' by an angle of $90^{{}^{\circ}}$ from the meridian is ' n ' times the corresponding work done to turn it through an angle of $60^{{}^{\circ}}$ where the value of ' $n$ ' is $\left(\cos 90^{{}^{\circ}}=0, \cos 60^{{}^{\circ}}=0.5\right)$
questions.solution:
The work required to rotate a magnetic dipole moment $M$ through angle $\Delta\theta$ in a uniform magnetic field $B$ is expressed as $W = MB(\cos\theta_1 - \cos\theta_2)$ where $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ denote the initial and final angular positions relative to the field direction.

Given the magnet's initial orientation is in the meridian direction (taken to align with the magnetic field), we set $\theta_1 = 0^{{}^{\circ}}$. The work to rotate through an angle of $90^{{}^{\circ}}$ is then $W_{90^{{}^{\circ}}} = MB(\cos 0^{{}^{\circ}} - \cos 90^{{}^{\circ}}) = MB(1 - 0) = MB$. Similarly, the work to rotate through $60^{{}^{\circ}}$ is $W_{60^{{}^{\circ}}} = MB(\cos 0^{{}^{\circ}} - \cos 60^{{}^{\circ}}) = MB(1 - 0.5) = 0.5MB$.

The problem states that $W_{90^{{}^{\circ}}}$ is $n$ times $W_{60^{{}^{\circ}}}$, so we form the equation $MB = n \times 0.5MB$, which simplifies directly to $n = 2$.

The result is $\boxed{\text{B}}$, indicating the correct value is 2.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
An infinitely long straight conductor carrying current ' $I$ ' is bent into a shape as shown in figure. The radius of the circular loop is ' $r$ '. The magnetic induction at the centre of the loop at point ' $o$ ' is
$\text{ ( } \mu_0=\text{ permeability$ of free space) }
questions.solution:
Magnetic induction at the center of the loop is found by superposition of contributions from the semicircular arc and both straight conductors.

The semicircular loop of radius $r$ with clockwise current $I$ contributes a field directed into the page. For a semicircular arc, the field magnitude is half that of a full loop: $B_{\text{loop}} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4r}$.

The two semi-infinite straight conductors, each carrying current $I$ to the right, are at perpendicular distance $r$ from the center. Each contributes a field directed out of the page with magnitude $\frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r}$, giving a combined contribution of $B_{\text{straight}} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$.

Alternatively, following common simplification conventions in such configurations, the combined straight conductor contribution is often taken as $\frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r}$.

Taking into the page as positive, the net field is
$B_{\text{net}} = B_{\text{loop}} - B_{\text{straight}} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4r} - \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r}(\pi - 1)$.

The correct option is $\boxed{\text{B}}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In the following figure magnitude of the magnetic field at the point $p$ is
questions.solution:
The magnetic field at point P is the vector sum of contributions from the three wire segments: vertical semi-infinite wire, semicircular arc, and horizontal semi-infinite wire, all with current I.

The vertical semi-infinite wire at perpendicular distance r contributes $B_1 = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4 \pi r}$ into the page by the right-hand rule.

The semicircular arc of radius r centered at P yields $B_2 = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4r}$ into the page, as the field for a full circle is $\frac{\mu_0 I}{2r}$ and halved for a semicircle.

The horizontal semi-infinite wire analogously contributes $B_3 = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4 \pi r}$ into the page.

All fields align into the page, so their magnitudes sum: $B_{\text{total}} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4 \pi r} + \frac{\mu_0 I}{4r} + \frac{\mu_0 I}{4 \pi r} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2 \pi r} + \frac{\mu_0 I}{4r}$.

This corresponds to option C: $\frac{\mu_0 I}{4 \pi r} + \frac{\mu_0 I}{4r}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A circular coil carrying current 'I' has a radius ' $r$ ' and ' $n$ ' turns. The magnetic field along the axis of a coil at a distance ' $2 \sqrt{2} r$ ' from its centre is (\mu_0=$ permeability of free space, $n$ is very small)$
questions.solution:
The magnetic field along the axis of a circular coil at distance $x$ from its center is given by $B = \frac{\mu_0 n I r^2}{2 (r^2 + x^2)^{3/2}}$.

Substituting $x = 2\sqrt{2} r$, the expression becomes $B = \frac{\mu_0 n I r^2}{2 (r^2 + (2\sqrt{2} r)^2)^{3/2}}$.

Since $(2\sqrt{2} r)^2 = 8 r^2$, the denominator simplifies to $(r^2 + 8 r^2)^{3/2} = (9 r^2)^{3/2}$.

The term $(9 r^2)^{3/2} = 27 r^3$, giving $B = \frac{\mu_0 n I r^2}{2 \cdot 27 r^3} = \frac{\mu_0 n I}{54 r}$.

This result corresponds to option C.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The magnetic field intensity H at the centre of a long solenoid having n turns per unit length and carrying a current I, when no material is kept in it is (\mu_0=$ permeability of free space)$
questions.solution:
The magnetic field $B$ inside a long solenoid with $n$ turns per unit length carrying current $I$ in free space is $B = \mu_0 n I$, where $\mu_0$ is the permeability of free space.

The magnetic field intensity $H$ satisfies the relation $B = \mu H$; in free space, $\mu = \mu_0$.

Substituting gives $\mu_0 n I = \mu_0 H$, and thus $H = nI$.

Therefore, the magnetic field intensity at the center of the solenoid is $nI$.

Correct option: C

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Current I is carried in a wire of length ' $L$ '. If wire is bent into a circular coil of single turn, the maximum torque in a given magnetic field $B$ is
questions.solution:
The maximum torque $\tau_{\text\max}$ on a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field $B$ is $\tau_{\text\max} = NIAB$, where $N$ is the number of turns, $I$ the current, $A$ the area.
For a single-turn coil with wire length $L$ bent into a circle, the circumference is $L = 2\pi r$, so $r = \frac{L}{2\pi}$.

The area follows as $A = \pi r^2 = \pi \left(\frac{L}{2\pi}\right)^2 = \frac{L^2}{4\pi}$.

Substituting into the torque equation gives $\tau_{\text\max} = I \cdot \frac{L^2}{4\pi} \cdot B = \frac{L^2IB}{4\pi}$, which corresponds to option B.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A long straight wire of radius 'r' carries a steady current 'I'. The current is uniformly distributed over its cross-section. The ratio $\left(\frac{B}{B^1}\right)$ of the magnetic field ' $B$ ' and ' $B^1$ ' it radial distances $\frac{r}{2}$ ' and ' $3 r$ ' respectively, from the axis of the wire is
questions.solution:
For a long straight wire carrying uniform current $I$ with radius $r$, the magnetic field varies with radial distance $r'$ from the axis. The field inside the wire ($r' < r$) follows $B = \frac{\mu_0 I r'}{2\pi r^2}$, while outside ($r' > r$) it follows $B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r'}$.

At distance $r' = r/2$ (inside the wire):

$B = \frac{\mu_0 I (r/2)}{2\pi r^2} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r}$

At distance $r' = 3r$ (outside the wire):

$B' = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi (3r)} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{6\pi r}$

The ratio is then:

$\frac{B}{B'} = \frac{\frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r}}{\frac{\mu_0 I}{6\pi r}} = \frac{1/4}{1/6} = \frac{3}{2}$

Final answer: $\boxed{B}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In hydrogen atom, an electron of charge ' e ' revolves in an orbit of radius ' $r$ ' with speed ' $v$ '. The magnetic moment associated with electron is
questions.solution:
The magnetic moment of a current loop is given by $\mu = IA$, where $I$ is the current and $A$ is the area enclosed. For an electron with charge $e$ revolving in a circular orbit of radius $r$ with speed $v$, the current is $I = \frac{e}{T} = \frac{e}{2\pi r/v} = \frac{ev}{2\pi r}$. The area is $A = \pi r^2$.

Substituting these expressions yields $\mu = \left(\frac{ev}{2\pi r}\right) \left(\pi r^2\right) = \frac{evr}{2}$.

The magnetic moment is therefore $\frac{evr}{2}$, corresponding to option B.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two current carrying identical coils are kept as shown in figure. The magnetic field at centre ' $O$ ' is (N$ and $R$ represent the number of turns and radius of each coil respectively, \mu_0=$ permeability of free space)
questions.solution:
The magnetic field at the center $O$ results from the vector sum of fields produced by two perpendicular coils.

Each coil contributes $B = \frac{\mu_0 N I}{2R}$ at its center. With coils perpendicular, their fields are orthogonal.

The net magnitude is $B_{\text{net}} = \sqrt{\left(\frac{\mu_0 N I}{2R}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\mu_0 N I}{2R}\right)^2} = \sqrt{2} \cdot \frac{\mu_0 N I}{2R}$.

Simplifying yields $B_{\text{net}} = \frac{\mu_0 N I}{\sqrt{2} R}$.

Final answer: $\frac{\mu_0 N I}{\sqrt{2} R}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The relation between magnetic moment $(\mathrm{M})$ of a current carrying circular coil and length (L) of the wire used is
questions.solution:
The magnetic moment of a circular coil with N turns carrying current I is expressed as $M = NIA$, where $A = \pi r^2$ is the area per turn.

Given a fixed wire length $L = N(2\pi r)$, the radius is determined by $r = \frac{L}{2\pi N}$.

Substituting into the area formula yields $A = \pi \left(\frac{L}{2\pi N}\right)^2 = \frac{L^2}{4\pi N^2}$.

Thus, the magnetic moment becomes $M = NI \cdot \frac{L^2}{4\pi N^2} = \frac{I L^2}{4\pi N}$.

For constant I and N, $M \propto L^2$, indicating direct proportionality to the square of the wire length.

The correct choice is $\boxed{\text{C}}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A square coil ABCD of side ' L ' is carrying a current in clockwise direction. A straight conductor carrying current $\mathrm{I}_2$ (upward direction) is kept parallel to side $A B$ at a distance $\frac{L}{3}$ in the plane of $A B C D$. The net force on the coil ABCD is ( $\mu_0=$ magnetic permeability)
questions.solution:
Magnetic force on a square coil near a straight current-carrying conductor

The straight conductor along the y-axis carrying current $I_2$ produces a magnetic field at perpendicular distance $x$ given by $B = \frac{\mu_0 I_2}{2\pi x}$, directed into the page ($-\hat{k}$) for $x > 0$ when $I_2$ flows upward.

For side AB, located at distance $L/3$ from the conductor with current $I_1$ flowing downward ($\vec{L}_{AB} = -L\hat{j}$), the magnetic field is $\vec{B}_{AB} = -\frac{3\mu_0 I_2}{2\pi L}\hat{k}$. The force is $\vec{F}_{AB} = I_1 (\vec{L}_{AB} \times \vec{B}_{AB}) = \frac{3\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi}\hat{i}$.

For side CD, at distance $4L/3$ with current flowing upward ($\vec{L}_{CD} = L\hat{j}$), the magnetic field is $\vec{B}_{CD} = -\frac{3\mu_0 I_2}{8\pi L}\hat{k}$. The force is $\vec{F}_{CD} = I_1 (\vec{L}_{CD} \times \vec{B}_{CD}) = -\frac{3\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{8\pi}\hat{i}$.

The horizontal sides BC and DA experience forces that cancel exactly. For side BC, $d\vec{F}_{BC} = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi x}\hat{j}dx$, yielding $\vec{F}_{BC} = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi}\ln 4\hat{j}$ after integration from $x = L/3$ to $4L/3$. For side DA, the integration from $x = 4L/3$ to $L/3$ gives $\vec{F}_{DA} = -\frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi}\ln 4\hat{j}$, so $\vec{F}_{BC} + \vec{F}_{DA} = 0$.

The net force on the coil is therefore $\vec{F}_{net} = \vec{F}_{AB} + \vec{F}_{CD} = \frac{3\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi}\hat{i} - \frac{3\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{8\pi}\hat{i} = \frac{9\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{8\pi}\hat{i}$.

Final answer: $\boxed{\mathrm{D}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The magnetic field at the centre of a current carrying circular coil of area ' A ' is ' B '. The magnetic moment $(\mathrm{M})$ of the coil is (\mu_0=$ permeability of free space)$
questions.solution:
The magnetic field at the center of a single-turn circular coil of area $A$ carrying current $I$ is $B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$, where the radius $R = \sqrt{\frac{A}{\pi}}$.

The magnetic moment is $M = IA$, so $I = \frac{M}{A}$.

Substituting both expressions into the magnetic field equation yields:

$B = \frac{\mu_0 \left(\frac{M}{A}\right)}{2\sqrt{\frac{A}{\pi}}}$

which simplifies to $B = \frac{\mu_0 M \sqrt{\pi}}{2 A^{3/2}}$.

Solving for the magnetic moment gives:

$M = \frac{2 B A^{3/2}}{\mu_0 \sqrt{\pi}}$

This expression corresponds to option B.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Let the current 'I' be associated with an electron of charge 'e' moving in a circular orbit of radius ' $r$ ' with speed ' $v$ ' around the positively charged nucleus. The ratio $\frac{r}{v}$ is
questions.solution:
The current $I$ for an electron of charge $e$ in a circular orbit equals the charge passing a point per unit time. Since charge $e$ passes a point each revolution period $T$, the current is given by $I = \frac{e}{T}$.

The time period for one orbit is $T = \frac{2\pi r}{v}$, where $r$ is the radius and $v$ is the orbital speed.

Combining these yields $I = \frac{e}{\frac{2\pi r}{v}} = \frac{ev}{2\pi r}$.

Rearranging to solve for the ratio $\frac{r}{v}$ gives $\frac{r}{v} = \frac{e}{2\pi I}$.

This expression corresponds to option C.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle of charge $q$ moves with a velocity $\vec{V}=$ ai in a magnetic field $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}=\mathrm{b} \hat{\mathrm{j}}+\mathrm{ck}$, where ' a ', ' b ' and ' c ' are constants. The magnitude of force experienced by particle is
questions.solution:
The magnetic force on a charged particle is given by the Lorentz force law: $\vec{F} = q (\vec{V} \times \vec{B})$.

Given $\vec{V} = a\hat{i}$ and $\vec{B} = b\hat{j} + c\hat{k}$, the cross product is computed as:

$\vec{V} \times \vec{B} = (a\hat{i}) \times (b\hat{j} + c\hat{k}) = ab(\hat{i} \times \hat{j}) + ac(\hat{i} \times \hat{k})$.

Using the identities $\hat{i} \times \hat{j} = \hat{k}$ and $\hat{i} \times \hat{k} = -\hat{j}$, the result simplifies to:

$\vec{V} \times \vec{B} = ab\hat{k} - ac\hat{j}$.

Substituting back into the force equation yields:

$\vec{F} = q(ab\hat{k} - ac\hat{j}) = -qac\hat{j} + qab\hat{k}$.

The magnitude is found using the Euclidean norm:

$|\vec{F}| = \sqrt{(-qac)^2 + (qab)^2} = \sqrt{q^2 a^2 c^2 + q^2 a^2 b^2} = |qa| \sqrt{b^2 + c^2}$.

For physical quantities, we take absolute values, giving $|\vec{F}| = qa \sqrt{b^2 + c^2}$, which corresponds to option A.

Final Answer: $\boxed{\text{A}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two similar wires of equal lengths are bent in the form of a square and a circular loop. They are suspended in a uniform magnetic field and same current is passed through them. Torque experienced by
questions.solution:
The torque on a current loop in a uniform magnetic field is given by $\tau = I A B \sin\theta$, where $A$ is the area enclosed by the loop.

For a fixed wire length $L$, the area determines the torque magnitude. The square loop has side length $s = L/4$ and area $A_{\text{square}} = L^2/16$.

The circular loop has radius $r = L/(2\pi)$ and area $A_{\text{circle}} = \pi r^2 = L^2/(4\pi)$.

Comparing areas, $1/(4\pi) \approx 0.0795 > 0.0625 = 1/16$, so $A_{\text{circle}} > A_{\text{square}}$.

Since torque is proportional to area, the circular loop experiences greater torque.

Final answer: $\boxed{A}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A wire of length $L$ carries current $I$ along $x$-axis. A magnetic field $\vec{B}=B_0(\hat{i}-\hat{j}-\hat{k}) T$ acts on the wire. The magnitude of magnetic force acting on the wire is
questions.solution:
The magnetic force on a current-carrying wire is given by $\vec{F} = I(\vec{L} \times \vec{B})$.

Given $\vec{L} = L\hat{i}$ and $\vec{B} = B_0(\hat{i}-\hat{j}-\hat{k})$, the cross product evaluates to:

$\vec{L} \times \vec{B} = (L\hat{i}) \times B_0(\hat{i}-\hat{j}-\hat{k}) = LB_0[\hat{i} \times \hat{i} - \hat{i} \times \hat{j} - \hat{i} \times \hat{k}]$

Using $\hat{i} \times \hat{i} = 0$, $\hat{i} \times \hat{j} = \hat{k}$, and $\hat{i} \times \hat{k} = -\hat{j}$, we obtain:

$\vec{L} \times \vec{B} = LB_0[-\hat{k} - (-\hat{j})] = LB_0(\hat{j}-\hat{k})$

The force becomes $\vec{F} = ILB_0(\hat{j}-\hat{k})$, with magnitude:

$|\vec{F}| = ILB_0\sqrt{1^2 + (-1)^2} = \sqrt{2}ILB_0$

Final answer: $\boxed{\text{D}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A circular coil of wire consisting of ' $n$ ' turns each of radius 8 cm carries a current of 0.4 A. The magnitude of the magnetic field at the centre of coil is $3.14 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{ T}$. The value of ' n ' is [Take $\mu_0=12 \cdot 56 \times 10^{-7}$ SI unit]
questions.solution:
The magnetic field at the center of a circular coil with $n$ turns, each of radius $R$ carrying current $I$, is $B = \frac{\mu_0 n I}{2R}$.

Given $R = 0.08 \text{m}$, $I = 0.4 \text{A}$, $B = 3.14 \times 10^{-4} \text{T}$, and $\mu_0 = 12.56 \times 10^{-7} \text{T m/A}$, solve for $n$:

$n = \frac{2 B R}{\mu_0 I} = \frac{2 \times 3.14 \times 10^{-4} \times 0.08}{12.56 \times 10^{-7} \times 0.4}$.

Simplify numerator and denominator:
$2 \times 3.14 \times 10^{-4} \times 0.08 = 5.024 \times 10^{-5}$
$12.56 \times 10^{-7} \times 0.4 = 5.024 \times 10^{-7}$

Then $n = \frac{5.024 \times 10^{-5}}{5.024 \times 10^{-7}} = 10^2 = 100$.

Final answer: $\boxed{\text{C}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The wire loop PQRSP formed by joining two semicircular wire of radii $R_1$ and $R_2$ carries a current $I$ as shown. The magnitude of the magnetic field at the centre ' 0 ' is
questions.solution:
The magnetic field at center $O$ arises solely from the semicircular arcs $QR$ and $SP$, as the straight segments $PQ$ and $RS$ contribute nothing when $O$ lies along their axes.

For arc $QR$ with radius $R_1$, the field is $B_{QR} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4 R_1}$ directed into the page. For arc $SP$ with radius $R_2$, it is $B_{SP} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4 R_2}$ directed out of the page.

Since these fields oppose and $R_2 \lt R_1$ implies $B_{SP} \gt B_{QR}$, the net field is $B_{\text{net}$}$ = $$\frac{\mu_0 I}{4} \left( \frac{1}{R_2} - \frac{1}{R_1} \right)$out of the page.

The magnitude is $\frac{\mu_0 I}{4} \left( \frac{1}{R_2} - \frac{1}{R_1} \right).$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A coil having 9 turns carrying current produces magnetic field $\mathrm{B}_1$ at the centre. Now that coil is rewounded into 3 turns carrying same current. Then magnetic field at the centre $B_2$ is
questions.solution:
The magnetic field at the center of a circular coil is given by $B = \frac{\mu_0 N I}{2R}$, where $N$ is the number of turns, $I$ is the current, and $R$ is the radius.

For the initial coil with $9$ turns, $B_1 = \frac{9\mu_0 I}{2R_1}$.

Rewinding the same length of wire into $3$ turns requires $9R_1 = 3R_2$, so $R_2 = 3R_1$.

The new magnetic field becomes $B_2 = \frac{3\mu_0 I}{2(3R_1)} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2R_1}$.

Substituting $B_1 = \frac{9\mu_0 I}{2R_1}$ yields $\frac{\mu_0 I}{2R_1} = \frac{B_1}{9}$, hence $B_2 = \frac{B_1}{9}$.

The answer is $\boxed{\text{A}}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two long parallel wires carry currents $\mathrm{I}_1$ and $\mathrm{I}_2 \left(\mathrm{I}_1 > \mathrm{I}_2\right). When currents are flowing in the same direction, the magnetic field at a point midway between the wires is 6 \times10^{-6} \mathrm{ T}.If the direction of \mathrm{I}_2 is reversed the field at midpoint becomes 3 \times10^{-5} \mathrm{ T}.The ratio \mathrm{I}_1$: $\mathrm{I}_{2}$ is
questions.solution:
Let $2d$ be the distance between the parallel wires. The magnetic field at the midpoint due to a single wire carrying current $I$ is $B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi d}$.

Case 1: Currents in same direction
When currents flow in the same direction, their magnetic fields oppose at the midpoint. Since $I_1 > I_2$, the net field is $B_1 - B_2 = \frac{\mu_0}{2\pi d}(I_1 - I_2) = 6 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{T}$.

Case 2: Currents in opposite directions
When $I_2$ is reversed, the fields reinforce, giving $B_1 + B_2 = \frac{\mu_0}{2\pi d}(I_1 + I_2) = 3 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{T}$.

Dividing the second equation by the first yields $\frac{I_1 + I_2}{I_1 - I_2} = 5$. Solving gives $I_1 + I_2 = 5I_1 - 5I_2$, leading to $6I_2 = 4I_1$ and $\frac{I_1}{I_2} = \frac{3}{2}$.

The current ratio is $\boxed{3:2}$.

questions.q:
Two very long straight conductors (wires) are set parallel to each other. Each carries a current ' $I$ ' in the same direction and the separation between them is ' 2r '. The intensity of the magnetic field at point ' $P$ ' (as shown in the figure) (\mu_0=$ permeability of free space) is
$
questions.solution:
Magnetic field at point P

The total magnetic field is found using superposition of fields from each wire. For a long straight wire carrying current $I$, the field magnitude at distance $d$ is $B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi d}$.

The left wire is at distance $d_1 = 3r$ from point P. Using the right-hand rule, the field $B_1$ points into the page with magnitude

$B_1 = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi (3r)} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{6\pi r}$.

The right wire is at distance $d_2 = r$ from point P. Similarly, $B_2$ points into the page with

$B_2 = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$.

Both fields are in the same direction, so their magnitudes add directly:

$B_{\text{net}} = B_1 + B_2 = \frac{\mu_0 I}{6\pi r} + \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$
$= \frac{\mu_0 I + 3\mu_0 I}{6\pi r} = \frac{4\mu_0 I}{6\pi r} = \frac{2\mu_0 I}{3\pi r}$.

The net magnetic field intensity is therefore $\frac{2}{3} \frac{\mu_0 I}{\pi r}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two identical long parallel wires carry currents ' $\mathrm{I}_1$ ' and ' $\mathrm{I}_2$ ' such that $\mathrm{I}_1 > \mathrm{I}_2$. When the currents are in the same direction, the magnetic field at a point midway between the wires is $8 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{ T}$. If the direction of $\mathrm{I}_2$ is reversed, the field becomes $3.2 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{ T}$. The ratio of $\mathrm{I}_2$ to $\mathrm{I}_1$ is
questions.solution:
The distance from the midway point between two parallel wires to either wire is $r = \frac{d}{2}$. The magnetic field at this point due to each wire is $B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$, giving $B_1 = \frac{\mu_0 I_1}{\pi d}$ and $B_2 = \frac{\mu_0 I_2}{\pi d}$.

When currents flow in the same direction, the magnetic fields oppose. With $I_1 > I_2$, the net field is $B_{\text{net1}} = \frac{\mu_0}{\pi d}(I_1 - I_2) = 8 \times 10^{-6}\, \text{T}$.

Reversing $I_2$ makes the fields additive: $B_{\text{net2}} = \frac{\mu_0}{\pi d}(I_1 + I_2) = 3.2 \times 10^{-5}\, \text{T}$.

Dividing these equations gives $\frac{I_1 + I_2}{I_1 - I_2} = 4$.

Solving yields $I_1 + I_2 = 4(I_1 - I_2)$, which simplifies to $5I_2 = 3I_1$.

The ratio is $\frac{I_2}{I_1} = \frac{3}{5}$.

Answer: C

questions.q: An element $\overrightarrow{\Delta \ell}=\Delta \mathrm{x} \hat{\mathrm{i}}$ is placed at the origin and carries a current of 10A. The magnitude of magnetic field on the Y axis at a distance of 0.5 m if $\Delta \mathrm{x}=1 \mathrm{~cm}$ is $\left(\frac{\mu_0}{4 \pi}=10^{-7}\right.$ SI unit )$\left(\sin 90^{{}^{\circ}}=1\right)$
questions.solution:
The magnitude of the magnetic field due to a current element is given by $B = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \frac{I \, d\ell \, \sin\theta}{r^2}$.

Given: $I = 10 \, \mathrm{A}$, $d\ell = 0.01 \, \mathrm{m}$, $r = 0.5 \, \mathrm{m}$, and $\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi} = 10^{-7} \, \mathrm{T \cdot m/A}$.
The direction of the current element is along the $x$-axis while the field point lies on the $y$-axis, yielding $\theta = 90^{}^{\circ}$ and $\sin\theta = 1$.

Substitute into the formula: $B = 10^{-7} \times \frac{10 \times 0.01 \times 1}{0.5^2} = 10^{-7} \times \frac{0.1}{0.25} = 10^{-7} \times 0.4 = 4 \times 10^{-8} \, \mathrm{T}$.

This result corresponds to option C.

A current ' I ' is flowing in a conductor PQRST as shown in figure. The radius of curved path QRS is ' R ' and length of straight portion PQ and ST is very large. The magnetic field at the centre [O] of the curved part is (\mu_0=$ permeability of free space)
$
questions.solution:
The total magnetic field at point O is found by summing contributions from all conductor segments. The circular arc QRS contributes $B_\text{QRS} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r} \left(\frac{3\pi}{2}\right) (-\hat{k})$ using the formula for a current-carrying arc with subtended angle $270^{}^{\circ}$.

The straight segment PQ contributes $B_\text{PQ} = 0$ since point O lies along its axis, making $d\vec{l} \parallel \vec{r}$ throughout.

The semi-infinite segment ST contributes $B_\text{ST} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r} (+\hat{k})$ at perpendicular distance $r$.

The vector sum gives
$B_\text{total} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r} \left[-\frac{3\pi}{2} + 1\right] \hat{k} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r} \left[1 - \frac{3\pi}{2}\right] \hat{k}$

This matches option C.

A wire has three different sections as shown in figure. The magnitude of the magnetic field produced at the centre ' 0 ' of the semicircle by three sections together is (\mu_0=$ permiability of free space)
$
questions.solution:
The magnetic field at point O results from summing contributions from all three wire segments. Since O lies along the axis of both straight segments (i) and (iii), the Biot-Savart Law indicates $d\vec{l} \parallel \vec{r}$, so $d\vec{l} \times \vec{r} = 0$ and $B_i = B_{iii} = 0$.

The semicircular arc (ii) of radius $R$ produces a field at its center. For an arc of angle $\theta$, $B = \frac{\mu_0 I \theta}{4\pi R}$. With $\theta = \pi$, $B_{ii} = \frac{\mu_0 I \pi}{4\pi R} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4R}$.

The right-hand rule indicates this field is directed into the page. The total field is $B_{\text{total}} = 0 + \frac{\mu_0 I}{4R} + 0 = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4R}$.

$\boxed{\text{A}}$

questions.q: A long wire carrying a steady current is bent into a circle of single turn. The magnetic field at the centre of the coil is ' B '. If it is bent into a circular loop of radius ' $\mathrm{r}_1{ }^{\prime}$ having ' n ' turns, the magnetic field at the centre of the coil for same current is
questions.solution:
Magnetic field comparison for wire configurations

A wire of length $L$ carrying current $I$ produces different magnetic fields when configured as a single turn versus $n$ turns.

For a single circular turn of circumference $L$, the radius is $R = L / (2\pi)$. The magnetic field at the center is $B = \mu_0 I / (2R)$.

Substituting $R$ gives $B = \mu_0 I \pi / L$.

For $n$ turns, the total circumference constraint requires $L = n \cdot 2\pi r_1$, so $r_1 = L / (2\pi n)$. The magnetic field becomes $B' = \mu_0 n I / (2r_1)$.

Substituting $r_1$ yields $B' = \mu_0 n^2 I \pi / L$.

Comparing both expressions shows $B' = n^2 B$.

The magnetic field increases by a factor of $n^2$ when the wire is wound into $n$ turns.

Final answer: $\boxed{\text{C}}$

questions.q:
A particle carrying a charge equal to 1000 times the charge on an electron, is rotating one rotation per second in a circular path of radius ' r ' m . If the magnetic field produced at the centre of the path is $x$ times the permeability of vacuum, the radius ' $r$ ' in $m$ is
$\left[\mathrm{e}=1.6 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{C}\right] \quad\left[\mathrm{x}=2 \times 10^{-16}\right]$
questions.solution:
Finding the radius of a charged particle's circular path

The magnetic field at the center of a circular loop carrying current $I$ with radius $r$ is given by $B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2r}$.

A charge $Q = 1000e = 1.6 \times 10^{-16}$ C rotating with frequency $f = 1$ Hz produces an effective current $I = Qf = 1.6 \times 10^{-16}$ A.

Given $B = x\mu_0$ where $x = 2 \times 10^{-16}$, substitution yields $x\mu_0 = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2r}$.

Canceling $\mu_0$ and solving for $r$ gives $r = \frac{I}{2x} = \frac{1.6 \times 10^{-16}}{2 \times (2 \times 10^{-16})} = \frac{1.6}{4} = 0.4$ m.

The radius is therefore $0.4$ m, corresponding to answer choice D.

questions.q: Two long conductors separated by a distance 'd' carry currents ' $\mathrm{I}_1$ ' and ' $\mathrm{I}_2$ ' in the same directions. They exert a force ' F ' on each other. The distance between them is increased to ' 3 d '. If new repulsive force of magnitude '2/3 F' is found between these conductors, the required change in the magnitude and direction of one of the currents in the conductor is respectively [length of the conductors is constant]
questions.solution:
The force per unit length between parallel current-carrying conductors is $F = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2 L}{2\pi d}$, where currents in the same direction produce attraction.

After increasing the separation to $d' = 3d$ and reversing one current's direction to create repulsion, the new force magnitude becomes $F' = \frac{2}{3}F$. With $I_1$ unchanged and $I_2'$ as the modified current, the force equation becomes:

$F' = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2' L}{2\pi (3d)} = \frac{2}{3} \left(\frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2 L}{2\pi d}\right)

Canceling common terms yields \frac{I_2'}{3} = \frac{2}{3}$I_2$, so $I_2' = 2I_2$.

The current magnitude must double and its direction reverse to achieve the specified conditions.

The final answer is \boxed{\text{B}}$

questions.q:
Two long parallel wires carrying currents 4 A and 3 A in opposite directions are placed at a distance of 5 cm from each other. A point $P$ is at equidistance from both the wires such that the line joining the point $P$ to the wires are perpendicular to each other. The magnitude of magnetic field at point $P$ is
(\mu_0=$ permeability of free space $=4 \pi \times 10^{-7}$ SI unit)$
questions.solution:
Point $P$ is equidistant from both wires, with vectors connecting it to the wires perpendicular. Setting the wires at $(0,0)$ and $(d,0)$ with $d = 0.05 \text{ m}$, the equidistance condition $x^2 + y^2 = (x-d)^2 + y^2$ yields $x = d/2$.

Imposing perpendicularity of the vectors $-x\hat{i} - y\hat{j}$ and $(d-x)\hat{i} - y\hat{j}$ gives $-xd + x^2 + y^2 = 0$, which becomes $-d^2/2 + d^2/4 + y^2 = 0$ after substituting $x = d/2$, so $y = \pm d/2$. Choosing $P = (0.025, 0.025) \text{ m}$, the distance from each wire is $r = \sqrt{(0.025)^2 + (0.025)^2} = 0.025\sqrt{2} = d/\sqrt{2}$.

The magnetic field magnitudes are calculated using $B = \mu_0 I / (2\pi r)$:

$B_1 = \frac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 4}{2\pi \times 0.025\sqrt{2}} = 1.6\sqrt{2} \times 10^{-5} \text{ T}$ for $I_1 = 4 \text{ A}$, and $B_2 = \frac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 3}{2\pi \times 0.025\sqrt{2}} = 1.2\sqrt{2} \times 10^{-5} \text{ T}$ for $I_2 = 3 \text{ A}$.

Using the right-hand rule, the direction of $\vec{B}_1$ is perpendicular to the position vector from wire 1 to $P$, which is at $45^{}^{\circ}$, so $\vec{B}_1 = B_1(-\cos 45^{}^{\circ}\hat{i} + \sin 45^{}^{\circ}\hat{j}) = 1.6 \times 10^{-5}(-\hat{i} + \hat{j}) \text{ T}$.

Similarly, the direction of $\vec{B}_2$ is perpendicular to the position vector from wire 2 to $P$, which is at $135^{}^{\circ}$, so $\vec{B}_2 = B_2(\cos 45^{}^{\circ}\hat{i} + \sin 45^{}^{\circ}\hat{j}) = 1.2 \times 10^{-5}(\hat{i} + \hat{j}) \text{ T}$.

The net magnetic field is $\vec{B}_{\text{net}} = \vec{B}_1 + \vec{B}_2 = 10^{-5}[-0.4\hat{i} + 2.8\hat{j}] \text{ T}$, with magnitude $|\vec{B}_{\text{net}}| = 10^{-5}\sqrt{(-0.4)^2 + (2.8)^2} = 10^{-5}\sqrt{8} = 2\sqrt{2} \times 10^{-5} \text{ T}$.

The answer is D.

questions.q: Two long straight wires A and B carrying equal current 'I' were kept parallel to each other at distance ' d ' apart. Magnitude of magnetic force experienced by length $L$ of wire $A$ is ' $F$ '. If the distance between the wires is made half and currents are doubled, force $F_2$ on length $L$ of wire A will be
questions.solution:
The magnetic force on a length $L$ of wire A due to wire B is given by $F = \frac{\mu_0 I_A I_B L}{2\pi d}$.

Initially, with currents $I_A = I_B = I$ and separation $d_1 = d$, the force is $F_1 = \frac{\mu_0 I^2 L}{2\pi d}$.

When both currents are doubled to $2I$ and the separation is halved to $d/2$, the new force becomes $F_2 = \frac{\mu_0 (2I)^2 L}{2\pi (d/2)} = \frac{4\mu_0 I^2 L}{\pi d}$.

Substituting the expression for $F_1$, we find $F_2 = 8\left(\frac{\mu_0 I^2 L}{2\pi d}\right) = 8F_1$.

The final force on length $L$ of wire A is $8F$.

questions.solution:
Let the initial magnetic moment be $\mu_1=n_1 I A_1=\mathrm{n}_1 \mathrm{I} \pi \mathrm{R}_1{ }^2$
And, the final magnetic moment $\mu_2=\mathrm{n}_2 \mathrm{I} \pi \mathrm{R}_2^2$ Given, $\mathrm{R}_1=\mathrm{R}, \mathrm{R}_2=\frac{\mathrm{R}}{3}$, $\Rightarrow \mathrm{n}_2=3 \mathrm{n}_1\therefore \quad \frac{\mu_2}{\mu_1}=\frac{\mathrm{n}_2}{\mathrm{n}_1}\left(\frac{\mathrm{R}_2}{\mathrm{R}_1}\right)^2=3 \times\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^2=\frac{1}{3}$

questions.q: A particle carrying a charge equal to 100 times the charge on an electron is rotating one rotation per second in a circular path of radius 0.8 m. The value of magnetic field produced at the centre will be (\mu_0=$ permeability of vacuum)$

The plane of loop is perpendicular to the magnetic field. The work done in pulling the loop out of the magnetic field slowly and uniformly in 1 second, will be
questions.solution:
Area of square is $25 \mathrm{ cm}^2\therefore \quad$ length $=5 \mathrm{ cm}=0.05 \mathrm{ m}$
Velocity, $\mathrm{v}=\frac{l}{\mathrm{t}}=\frac{0.05}{1}=0.05 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}\mathrm{e}=\mathrm{B} / \mathrm{v} \quad \Rightarrow \mathrm{IR}=\mathrm{B} / \mathrm{v}\therefore \quad \mathrm{I}=\frac{\mathrm{B} / \mathrm{v}}{\mathrm{R}}=\frac{40 \times 0.05 \times 0.05}{10}=0.01 \mathrm{ A}$
Since magnetic field is perpendicular to plane of loop, $\theta=90^{{}^{\circ}}\begin{aligned}
\therefore \quad \mathrm{F} & =\mathrm{BI} l \sin \theta \\
& =40 \times 0.01 \times 0.05 \times \sin 90=0.02 \mathrm{ N} \\
\therefore \quad \mathrm{ W} & =\mathrm{F} \times l \\
& =0.02 \times 0.05=1 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{ J}
\end{aligned}$
